articles.title: Middle East and Europe - Food Security Outlook : Risk of Famine (IPC Phase 5) in Yemen’s Ta’izz City; Crisis outcomes persist regionwide, October 2026 - May 2027
articles.description: Please refer to the attached file. Key Messages Persistent insecurity, weak purchasing power, and constrained livelihoods are expected to sustain Emergency (IPC Phase 4) outcomes in western Yemen and Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes across conflict-affected areas of Lebanon, Syria, and Ukraine through May 2027. In Yemen, Emergency (IPC Phase 4) outcomes are expected in Al-Hudaydah, Hajjah, Ta'izz, and Lahij governorates, with Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes elsewhere. A portion of households in frontline governorates, including Ta’izz and Lahij, are likely experiencing Catastrophe (IPC Phase 5), and there is a crediblerisk of Famine (IPC Phase 5) in besieged Ta’izz City between February and May if siege conditions persist and tighten. In Lebanon, Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes are expected across much of the south, Baalbek–El-Hermel, Bekaa, and northern areas despite improved conditions since June. In Syria, Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes are expected across Northeast Syria (NES), Northwest Syria (NWS), and Latakia, where declining income-earning opportunities and high food and living costs continue to constrain household food access despite improved agricultural production. In Ukraine, Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes will likely persist in the most conflict-affected frontline and occupied areas, with some areas likely deteriorating from Stressed! (IPC Phase 2!) to Crisis (IPC Phase 3) between February and May. Conflict and insecurity continue to disrupt livelihoods, displace populations, and constrain physical access to food and income across the region. In Yemen, intensified fighting, particularly around Ta'izz and Lahij, is driving new displacement, disrupting commercial supply routes, limiting mobility and access to livelihoods and markets, and restricting market functionality across frontline areas. Food inflows into besieged Ta’izz City are severely restricted. In Lebanon, although hostilities have declined substantially since the peak escalation period, continued Israeli military activity, demolitions, and movement restrictions within and near the southern security zone are preventing sustainable returns and restricting access to agricultural land and livelihoods. In Syria, localized insecurity continues to disrupt agricultural and livestock activities, while large-scale returns place additional pressure on housing, services, and already limited employment opportunities. In Ukraine, attacks on critical infrastructure, displacement, and restricted access to agricultural land and markets continue to constrain livelihoods and food access among frontline populations. Weak household purchasing power remains a common regional challenge, as high food and essential living costs outpace limited income-earning opportunities, even where markets are adequately supplied. In Syria, sharply rising diesel prices, currency depreciation, and elevated food and heating costs are expected to erode purchasing power, particularly during the January–April lean season. Despite an above-average 2026 cereal harvest, high production costs and limited agricultural labor opportunities are reducing income gains for poor households. In Lebanon, high food and fuel prices, weak labor demand, and continued economic contraction are expected to constrain food access despite broadly functional markets. In Yemen, economic fragmentation, conflict-related disruptions, heavy taxation in areas under the control of the Sana’a-based authorities (SBA), and public budget deficits in areas controlled by the internationally recognized government (IRG) limit households’ ability to earn income, while high import dependence and inflationary pressures continue to undermine household purchasing power. In Ukraine, elevated food, energy, and transportation costs, alongside declining agricultural profitability and reduced labor opportunities, disproportionately affect pensioners, internally displaced persons (IDPs), and rural households near the front lines. Across the region, the primary challenge for most households remains financial access to food rather than national food availability. Winter and seasonal livelihood pressures are expected to further constrain food access, although the timing and severity of deterioration vary by country. In Syria, declining agricultural and casual labor opportunities, rising heating expenditures, and reduced household incomes are expected to widen food consumption gaps during the January–April lean season. In Lebanon, higher winter expenditures between December and March and below-average labor demand are expected to continue constraining household purchasing power. In Ukraine, winter heating, electricity, and transportation costs, compounded by attacks on energy infrastructure, will likely increase pressure on household budgets from January to March, forcing poor households to divert resources away from food purchases. Conditions are expected to improve by May as winter-related constraints ease and seasonal agricultural activities resume. In Yemen, anticipated seasonal improvements in food availability and access in less conflict-affected areas are expected to provide some relief, though continued fighting and restrictions on commercial supply routes will continue to constrain food access in frontline areas. Funding shortfalls and humanitarian access constraints are limiting the reach and effectiveness of humanitarian assistance. In Syria, reduced humanitarian food assistance and bread support will limit households' ability to mitigate food consumption gaps as seasonal incomes decline and winter expenditures increase. In Lebanon, assistance coverage is expected to decrease amid funding shortfalls and insecurity-related access constraints. In Yemen, assistance remains suspended in SBA-controlled areas, while funding shortfalls and access constraints in areas of active conflict are limiting food assistance delivery in IRG-controlled areas. In Ukraine, assistance will remain concentrated in frontline areas, though insecurity, winter conditions, and rising logistical costs are expected to complicate delivery to hard-to-reach populations. This regional report summarizes the analysis presented in FEWS NET’s country-level Food Security Outlooks for October 2026 - May 2027.
